title: Planning for a divided government: Contract terms to check now
summary: Divided government creates three funding scenarios for federal contractors. Learn which contract terms control your backlog exposure and recovery options now.
body_markdown:
The 2026 midterms produced a divided government, which can make budget agreements harder to reach. When Congress misses its budget deadline, it typically passes a continuing resolution (CR), temporary funding legislation that typically keeps agencies at prior-year levels for a set period and bars activities not funded the year before. For contractors, that can mean delayed new awards, which slow your pipeline, and funding that is assured only for the period the CR covers, which limits how much of your backlog you can perform and bill.


On November 10, 2026,[Washington Technology reported on remarks by Ira Entis](https://www.washingtontechnology.com/contracts/2026/11/accenture-leidos-execs-how-survive-divided-government/417155/) , chief strategy officer of Accenture Federal Services, and Rich Wilson, senior vice president of health and services growth at Leidos, at GovExec's After the Midterms event. Both spoke about how government contractors can prepare for a divided government. Entis urged them to build three plans:


- A traditional plan with "lumpy" funding under a CR.
- A harder plan with disruptions, funding pullbacks, and customer cancellations.
- A favorable plan in which money flows to AI, cyber, and Defense Department priorities.


Both executives also told contractors to be selective and make bid/no-bid calls quickly. They described a move from labor-based and cost-plus contracts toward outcome-based procurements, and Wilson spoke favorably about other transaction authorities (OTAs) and pilots.


Whichever scenario unfolds, the contract terms you have signed determine how much work in your backlog you must perform and what you can bill or recover if funding slows or stops. The terms in the bids you are pursuing do the same for your pipeline. The table below maps each scenario to affected terms.


Scenario Contract Terms


Lumpy CR funding Incremental funding, limitation-of-funds notices, option exercise, subcontract payment timing


Pullbacks and cancellations Stop-work orders, termination for convenience settlements, subcontract flow-downs


Money moves to AI, cyber, and DoD New awards, often OTAs and pilots, with negotiated data rights and milestone payments


## Incremental Funding


Incremental funding means the Government has obligated only part of the contract's value. A clause in the contract, such as Limitation of Funds, caps both what you must perform and what the Government must pay at that amount. Under a CR, this funding clause is often the first to affect your work. The funded amount, not the total contract value, tells you how much of your backlog is funded, meaning work you can perform and bill now.


One common mistake is assuming the Government has committed to pay the total contract value. On an incrementally funded contract, the full value is a ceiling. This means that the Government has obligated only the funded amount so far, and only for the period that amount covers. Counting the full value as backlog you can rely on overstates it.


Which funding clause your contract carries depends on contract type and agency. Incrementally funded cost-reimbursement contracts carry FAR 52.232-22 (Limitation of Funds). Its standard trigger is a written notice when costs expected over the next 60 days would push total costs past 75 percent of the funded amount (which the clause calls the amount allotted to the contract), and the contracting officer can vary those figures (30 to 90 days, 75 to 85 percent). Incrementally funded DoD fixed-price contracts carry DFARS 252.232-7007 (Limitation of Government's Obligation), under which you are not authorized to continue work on those items beyond the funded amount, and costs beyond it are at your risk. DoD generally requires fixed-price contracts to be fully funded, with narrow exceptions (DFARS 232.703-1), so that clause is less common. Contracts started before new fiscal-year funds arrive may instead carry FAR 52.232-18 (Availability of Funds), which makes the Government's obligation contingent on appropriated funds being available. FAR 32.703-2 generally bars the Government from accepting supplies or services until the contracting officer has told you in writing that funds are available. Certain one-year indefinite-quantity or requirements contracts for services, funded by annual appropriations and running past the first fiscal year, carry FAR 52.232-19 (Availability of Funds for the Next Fiscal Year).


The exact notice triggers and consequences are set by the clause in your contract, which may differ from the standard version. We recommend reviewing the following:


1. **The funded amount and the period it covers.** Compare it to your actual burn rate, not your invoicing schedule, and use it to separate funded backlog from unfunded backlog.
2. **The notice trigger.** These clauses generally require written notice to the contracting officer as costs approach the funded amount. Put that date on a calendar tied to burn rate.
3. **Your authority to keep working.** Costs you incur beyond the funded amount are generally at your own risk, so decide in advance who can approve working ahead of funding and under what conditions.


## Responding to a Stop-Work Order


Where your contract carries the stop-work clause (commonly FAR 52.242-15), the contracting officer can order you to pause all or part of the work for a limited period. If you receive a stop-work order, comply immediately and start protecting your right to cost and schedule relief from day one. The standard clause sets a stop period of up to 90 days, which the contracting officer can set shorter and the parties can extend by agreement. Within that period, the Government must cancel the order or terminate the affected work for default or convenience.


You must assert your right to an equitable adjustment within 30 days after the stoppage ends, though the contracting officer may act on a later request if the facts justify it. Do not rely on that discretion. On cost-reimbursement contracts the adjustment can reach estimated cost and fee.


How much you recover through an equitable adjustment depends on how well you can document the costs caused by the stoppage.We recommend putting three things in place before a stop-work order arrives:


- A separate charge code for stop-work costs, opened the day the order arrives.
- A named owner for the request for equitable adjustment and a calendar entry for its deadline.
- A same-day process to pass the order down to subcontractors, since their costs keep running too.


Not every contract includes a stop-work clause, so check that yours does. Terms vary by contract type, agency, and vehicle, and a missing or modified clause changes your options. A stop-work order does not by itself remove work from your backlog, but it can delay when you can perform and bill it, so reflect that in your cash forecast.


## Termination for Convenience Readiness


Are you ready to settle a termination for convenience? Many contractors are not. A termination replaces the unperformed part of that contract’s backlog with a settlement claim, and a strong settlement depends on records that have to be in place before the termination notice arrives. FAR Part 49 governs terminations of most non-commercial contracts, and the standard clauses (FAR 52.249-2 for fixed-price, FAR 52.249-6 for cost-reimbursement) let the Government end the work without any default by you.


Many IT contracts, however, are commercial contracts, governed by FAR 52.212-4(l) and FAR 12.403 rather than the Part 49 procedures. Under the commercial clause, on fixed-price work you are paid a percentage of the contract price that reflects the work performed. On labor-hour work you are paid for direct labor hours at the contract rates. Either way, you can also recover charges you can demonstrate, to the Government's satisfaction and using your standard record-keeping system, resulted from the termination. The parties generally agree on what the termination proposal must contain.


Under the Part 49 clauses, recovery is built from costs of work performed, reasonable settlement expenses, and amounts owed to terminated subcontractors. FAR 49.202 allows profit on work done and preparations made, but not anticipatory profits or consequential damages, and FAR 49.203 bars profit where the contract would have lost money.


Today, the standard fixed-price clause gives you one year from the effective date of termination to submit the final settlement proposal, and 120 days for inventory schedules, unless extended. DoD contracting officers currently follow a revised Part 49 under Class Deviation 2026-O0010 (effective February 1, 2026), which retains those same periods.


If you miss the deadline and do not ask for more time, you lose the right to appeal a settlement the contracting officer sets by determination. These deadlines may soon be shorter. A proposed rule published June 23, 2026 (FAR Case 2026-007, 91 Fed. Reg. 37698) would cut the proposal deadline to 90 days, inventory schedules to 60 days, and extension requests to 60 days. As of early November 2026, the rule had not been finalized, so the one-year period still applies, but a final rule could arrive soon.


Whatever deadline applies, and especially if it drops to 90 days, we recommend having four things ready before a termination notice arrives:


- **Cost records** that separate each contract and line item, so you can show incurred costs without a forensic project.
- **A subcontract map** listing every commitment, its status, and its termination terms.
- **Inventory and work in process** tied to specific contracts.
- **A milestone valuation rule.** On outcome-based or milestone-paid work, check how the contract treats effort on a milestone that is unfinished at termination. The milestone price may not be the number the settlement uses.


A good first step is a practice run: treat your largest incrementally funded contract as if it had just been terminated and time how long it takes to draft a settlement proposal.


If you work on a large DoD program, check two more DFARS terms. For major defense programs, DFARS 252.249-7002 requires you to notify affected employees and state and local officials within two weeks after the contracting officer tells you funding will be terminated or substantially reduced. You must also notify first-tier subcontractors above a dollar threshold within 60 days after you receive the contracting officer’s notice. For incrementally funded contracts running two years or more, with more than $25 million in research and development financing or $100 million in production investment, the agency head may approve DFARS 252.249-7000 (Special Termination Costs), which caps a reserve for items such as severance.


## Option Exercise Under a CR


Option exercise can become riskier under a CR. Exercising an option is the Government's right, not a commitment to you, so uncertain funding can delay or change that decision. That makes unexercised options a gray area between backlog and pipeline: awarded, but not committed. If the option goes unexercised, your contract generally provides no remedy.


Much of that risk comes down to timing and price. You can review four items in advance:


1. **Map every option.** List the exercise date, the notice period, and the option price for each contract. The standard option-to-extend clause (FAR 52.217-9) calls for preliminary written notice of intent to extend, typically 60 days before expiration, and that notice does not commit the Government. Do not treat it as a decision.
2. **Find your gap-filler.** Some contracts include a short-term extension of services clause (FAR 52.217-8, up to six months in total at the contract rates, which can change only for revisions to prevailing labor rates) that lets the Government bridge a gap. Know whether yours does, and for how long.
3. **Check the price you are held to.** Option prices were set at award. If exercise slips, compare those prices to your current labor and subcontract costs, and look for any price adjustment mechanism.
4. **Forecast honestly.** Treat unexercised options as probability-weighted revenue, not backlog, and decide how long you will carry staff against an option that has not been exercised.


## Carrying the Funding Gap for Subcontractors


Who carries the funding gap when subcontractors are involved? Unless your subcontracts say otherwise, you do. The Government's funding limits bind you, but they do not automatically bind your subcontractors, so a mismatch between the prime contract and the subcontract can leave you owing money you have not been paid.


Check these four points in your subcontract templates and active subcontracts:


1. **Funding flow-downs.** Does the subcontractor know its funded amount and its own notice duties? If not, it can run up costs you cannot bill.
2. **Stop-work and termination timing.** Your subcontractor's deadline to submit an adjustment or settlement request should fall before yours, so you can package it into your own submission.
3. **Payment conditions.** A pay-when-paid or pay-if-paid clause can shift the funding delay to the subcontractor, but how courts read these clauses varies by state and by drafting. Some states limit or void pay-if-paid clauses, so check the governing state law.
4. **Pass-through work.** Where you resell a subcontractor's work with little markup, a delayed Government payment means you are financing their cash flow. Confirm that you can actually afford that, and that the subcontract says what happens if payment is late.


Fixing these terms in your subcontract templates now is far less costly than resolving a mismatch during a stop-work order.


## OTAs and Pilots


When the deal is an other transaction agreement (an OTA, or OT in DoD usage) or a pilot, your rights depend almost entirely on the agreement’s own terms. An OTA is generally not a standard FAR-based procurement contract, so protections you take for granted, such as the termination framework in FAR Part 49 or default data-rights licenses, exist only if the agreement includes them.


Some statutory requirements still apply to DoD prototype OTs, including Comptroller General records access and the procurement integrity rules. DoD prototype OTs rest on 10 U.S.C. 4022, and other agencies use their own authorities. DoD's OT Guide says the FAR, the DFARS, and the Competition in Contracting Act do not apply to OTs, and that the Government has more flexibility to negotiate IP terms than in a traditional contract. Section 4022 counts a pilot or novel application of commercial technologies for defense purposes as a prototype project.


Wilson described OTAs and pilots as positives for the customer and for industry. If funding does flow to AI, cyber, and DoD priorities, some of your new pipeline may arrive in this form. Because the agreement sets your rights, any protection you need must be negotiated into it. Pay attention to the following terms:


1. **Termination and funding.** What happens to payment if funding is cut mid-milestone? Do not assume a FAR settlement process. If the agreement doesn’t set what you are paid on termination, negotiate a provision that does. DoD's guide recommends that most OT agreements let the Government terminate for insufficient funding, and it notes that termination does not automatically entitle the other party to payment for effort already spent. OTs are also not subject to the Contract Disputes Act, so check how disputes get resolved.
2. **Data rights and IP.** Define what you owned before the work, what gets developed, and what license the Government receives in each. Gaps in the text may not be filled by FAR or DFARS defaults. For AI work, spell out ownership and licensing of training data, model weights, fine-tuning materials, improvements, and outputs, and keep pre-existing technology distinct from project-specific developments.
3. **Pilot-to-production scope.** A pilot price should not quietly carry production-scale rights. Tie the license scope to what the Government is buying.
4. **Milestone acceptance.** Define acceptance criteria, how long the Government has to accept, and what happens to payment if acceptance stalls. DoD's guide notes that optional milestones become part of the agreement only if the Government exercises and funds them.
5. **Follow-on production.** Section 4022(f) allows a follow-on production award without further competition only if competitive procedures were used to select the participants and the prototype was successfully completed. That can include an individual prototype or subproject within a consortium, without waiting for every consortium activity to finish. If the prototype was not competitively awarded, do not count on follow-on production in your pipeline. Define how success will be judged, and the likely production scope, pricing, and IP rights, before the prototype begins.
6. **Audit access.** For a prototype OT paying more than $5 million, Section 4022(c) requires a clause giving the Comptroller General access to the records of the parties and participants. The requirement does not apply to a party with no other audit-access agreement with a Government entity in the prior year, and the head of the contracting activity can waive it after notifying Congress and the Comptroller General. Know what records could be reached before you sign, especially proprietary technology and subcontractor records.


## A Faster Bid/No-Bid Risk Screen


A faster bid/no-bid risk screen is a short set of contract-term questions that one person can answer from the solicitation in a day, with a decision rule set in advance. Both executives had advised contractors to be selective and decide quickly; a fixed screen makes those quick decisions possible by standardizing the legal and finance questions for every bid in your pipeline.


Screen question Green Red


Funding Funded for the first period at your planned staffing level Funded amount is below your ramp, with the rest uncertain


Stop-work and termination Stop-work adjustment rights and defined termination compensation, with deadlines you can meet Modified or waived protections, unclear recovery rights, or deadlines you could not meet


Payment trigger Paid on incurred cost or clear deliverables Paid on outcomes or milestones with vague acceptance terms


Options Base period recovers your bid and startup cost Margin depends on options being exercised


Subcontractors You can match funding, termination, and payment terms back to back You finance a pass-through or cannot flow terms down


Data rights and IP Scoped to the deliverables Broad, unclear, or reaching your pre-existing IP


Strategic fit Work you would invest in under all three scenarios Only works if the favorable scenario happens


The last row reflects Entis’s advice to invest in work that is critical under every scenario. We recommend deciding in advance how many red answers send a bid to legal review and how many lead to a no-bid, since a threshold set before deadline pressure is easier to apply consistently.


## Steps to Take Now


Review the places where funding risk becomes contract risk, and write down ahead of time what you will do in each of the three scenarios. Then prepare by organizing records and updating templates. Here are some key steps we recommend beginning with:


**1. Pull the funded amount and notice trigger for every incrementally funded contract.** Compare each to your current burn rate and your funded backlog, and calendar the notice dates.


**2. Build a stop-work protocol.** Name an owner, open a charge code on day one, and set a same-day flow-down to subcontractors.


**3. Run a termination settlement tabletop.** First confirm which termination rules govern each contract: the codified clause, an agency class deviation, or the commercial clause. Then use your largest incrementally funded contract, time a first-draft settlement proposal, and test whether you could meet a 90-day deadline in case the proposed rule is finalized.


**4. Map your options.** List each exercise date, notice period, option price, and any short-term extension clause.


**5. Align your subcontract templates.** Check funding flow-downs, claim deadlines that run ahead of your own, and payment conditions.


**6. Review your OTA and pilot terms.** Look at termination, data rights, milestone acceptance, and follow-on production language.


**7. Adopt a bid/no-bid screen with a written threshold.** Use the questions above on every opportunity in your pipeline and decide in advance what counts as too many red answers.


**8. Stress-test your backlog and pipeline forecast against all three scenarios.** Weight unexercised options as probabilities, not backlog, and set staffing triggers for each scenario.


If these raise questions about a contract you hold or are bidding on, General Legal’s Defense Tech & Government Contracts team can review specific clauses or help you plan how each scenario could affect your business.

Key takeaways


- •


The 2026 midterms created a divided government that can delay budget agreements, potentially resulting in continuing resolutions that freeze new contract awards and limit billable work.


- •


Government contractors should prepare three distinct funding scenarios: lumpy CR funding, disruptions with pullbacks and cancellations, and favorable funding for AI, cyber, and Defense priorities.


- •


Contract terms already signed determine how much backlog work contractors must perform and what they can bill if government funding slows or stops.


- •


Industry leaders recommend contractors become more selective with bids, make quicker bid/no-bid decisions, and prepare for a shift from cost-plus to outcome-based contracts.


- •


The specific terms in existing contracts and pending bids directly control a contractor's exposure and recovery options under each funding scenario.


TL;DR


Divided government impact 2026 midterms created budget uncertainty; continuing resolutions can delay awards and limit billable backlog


Three planning scenarios Prepare for lumpy CR funding, disruptions with cancellations, or favorable funding for AI/cyber/Defense


Contract terms matter Existing contract language determines what you must perform and can bill when funding changes


Bid strategy shift Be selective, make faster bid/no-bid calls as procurement moves toward outcome-based models


New procurement vehicles OTAs and pilots gaining favor as alternatives to traditional cost-plus contracts


Risk management Review contract terms now to understand exposure across all three funding scenarios


FAQs


### Does a continuing resolution change my contract terms?


No. A continuing resolution does not rewrite your contract, but lumpy funding can trigger the funding, option, and notice clauses you already signed. It can also slow the new awards your pipeline depends on.


### Which clause should I check first?


The funding clause on any incrementally funded contract. Find the funded amount and the point at which you must give the contracting officer notice.


### Can the Government pause my work without ending the contract?


Often, yes. A stop-work clause lets the contracting officer pause work for a limited period, and you should track those costs separately from the first day.


### What can I generally recover in a termination for convenience?


Costs of work performed, reasonable settlement expenses, subcontract settlements, and profit on work done, but not anticipatory profits or consequential damages, under the Part 49 clauses. Commercial contracts use a different formula. The proposal deadline is currently one year, including under DoD's class deviation, but a proposed rule would cut it to 90 days. In either case, the deadline that applies to you is the one written in your contract’s clause.


### Does an OTA come with the FAR protections I am used to?


Generally not. The agreement is the rulebook, so read its termination, payment, and data-rights terms as if nothing else will fill the gaps.
